hero.title: Glossary
hero.subtitle: Key concepts explained simply. From SHA-256 to Zero-Knowledge Proofs.

sha256.def: A cryptographic hash function that produces a 256-bit (64 character) hexadecimal fingerprint. Used by Satohash to create a unique identifier for each document without exposing its contents.

ots.def: A protocol that creates timestamp proofs by embedding document hashes into Merkle trees, which are then anchored to the Bitcoin blockchain via a single transaction.

merkleTree.def: A data structure where each leaf node is a hash and each non-leaf node is the hash of its children. OTS aggregates many timestamps into one Merkle tree before anchoring to Bitcoin.

otsFile.def: The proof file generated by Satohash containing the timestamp information. It is useless without the original document but can be verified independently using the open-source ots tool.

bitcoinBlockchain.def: A decentralized, immutable public ledger maintained by a global network of miners. Satohash anchors proof fingerprints into Bitcoin blocks for permanent timestamping.

blockHeight.def: The sequential number of a block in the Bitcoin blockchain. Each new block is assigned height + 1. The block height at the time of timestamping provides temporal proof.

nip05.def: Nostr Improvement Proposal #05 — maps a human-readable identifier (like user@domain.com) to a Nostr public key, enabling verifiable identity without sharing raw public keys.

nostr.def: A decentralized, censorship-resistant protocol for social networking and communication. Used by Satohash for identity verification and agent communication.

bolt12.def: A Lightning Network proposal for reusable, one-click offers. Enables recurring payments and metered access without repeated invoice generation.

lightning.def: A second-layer payment protocol on top of Bitcoin enabling instant, low-fee transactions. Used by Satohash for premium billing.

zeroKnowledge.def: A method to prove knowledge of information without revealing the information itself. In Satohash, your documents never leave your device — only their hashes are shared.

foss.def: Free and Open Source Software. Satohash is MIT-licensed and the full source code is publicly available on GitHub.

eidas.def: Electronic Identification, Authentication and Trust Services — an EU regulation that sets standards for electronic signatures and timestamping. Satohash proofs are eIDAS-compatible.

esign.def: The United States federal law that establishes the legal validity of electronic signatures and records. Satohash proofs comply with ESIGN requirements.

blockTime.def: The average time between Bitcoin blocks (approximately 10 minutes). The timestamp of the block containing your proof determines the notarization time.

mempool.def: The pool of unconfirmed Bitcoin transactions waiting to be included in a block. Satohash monitors the mempool for real-time network intelligence.

l402.def: A protocol standard for API authentication and metering using the Lightning Network. Enables pay-per-use access to premium features.

pwa.def: Progressive Web App — a web application that can be installed on a device and work offline. Satohash is a PWA with service worker caching.

what.label: 01 — What we do
what.title: What we do
what.p1: Satohash provides independent, cryptographic proof of existence for any digital file—contracts, photographs, source code, AI model outputs, web captures, or audit packages. We do not store or review the underlying content. Instead, we enable organizations and individuals to bind a mathematical fingerprint of that content to the Bitcoin blockchain via the open OpenTimestamps protocol, producing a portable proof that third parties can verify without trusting Satohash as a custodian of truth.
what.p2: In practical terms: when a document, delivery package, or digital artifact must later withstand scrutiny—from counterparties, regulators, courts, or internal audit—Satohash supplies a durable, non-repudiable record that the artifact existed in a specific form at a specific time. The service is designed for everyday use at the edge of work (legal, creative, investigative, and operational), not as a one-off novelty.

how.label: 02 — How it works
how.title: How it works
how.p1: The process is deliberately simple and privacy-preserving. First, the user’s browser (or approved client) computes a SHA-256 hash of the file using standard web cryptography; the original bytes need never leave the device. Second, only that 64-character hash is submitted to OpenTimestamps calendars, which aggregate many hashes into a Merkle tree and periodically commit the root into a Bitcoin transaction. Third, once a Bitcoin block confirms that commitment — typically about 60 minutes — the resulting .ots proof can be downloaded, archived, and independently verified with open-source tools and public chain data.
how.p2: Today, stamping is offered at no charge to the user. The economic model for Bitcoin network fees is absorbed at the calendar and protocol layer through batching; Satohash’s product cost is hosting and operations. When commercial tiers are introduced, settlement is expected via Lightning to Satohash—not a change of ledger. The proof remains anchored to Bitcoin either way.

truth.label: 03 — Truth
truth.title: Why this matters for truth
truth.p1: In an environment of generative media, deepfakes, disputed emails, and rewritten “sources of record,” the hardest question is often not what someone claims, but when a specific digital state first existed and whether it has been altered since. Institutional trust—brand statements, screenshots, and “our system says so”—is increasingly insufficient for adversarial settings. Cryptographic timestamping does not decide guilt or innocence; it restores a shared, machine-checkable baseline of temporal truth: this exact fingerprint was committed to a public, high-cost-to-rewrite ledger at this block height.
truth.p2: That baseline is essential for free expression, journalism, intellectual property priority, and civil process. Without it, history is negotiable. With it, parties may still disagree on meaning—but not on whether the bytes were present in the past. Satohash exists to make that property of Bitcoin available to non-specialists as a daily instrument of integrity. It proves when, not who.

enterprises.label: 04 — Enterprises
enterprises.title: For companies and institutional metrics
enterprises.p1: Enterprises adopt Satohash where audit trails, vendor disputes, regulatory examinations, and multi-party workflows demand evidence that is portable outside any single SaaS silo. Typical patterns include stamping executed agreements and board materials at signature; sealing software releases and configuration snapshots for change-control; anchoring investigative exports and customer communications; and instrumenting APIs so automated systems emit proofs as first-class artifacts. Because verification does not require ongoing access to Satohash infrastructure, the organization retains resilience if vendors change—or if Satohash itself is unavailable.
enterprises.p2: From a metrics perspective, leadership can treat proof coverage as an operational KPI: percentage of high-risk documents stamped within SLA; median time from document finalization to confirmed Bitcoin anchor; share of disputes closed with a verifiable .ots package; and family-product attribution of stamp volume by business unit or client system. These indicators align legal readiness with engineering practice—turning “we keep records” into “we can prove, independently, what existed when.” Charts on this page are illustrations, not live billing metrics.

onboardingWelcomePage.heroSubtitle: Satohash provides mathematically indisputable proof of existence for your most critical documents. Local privacy, global immutability.

proof.insight: SHA-256 Hashing: Every document gets a unique 64-character 'fingerprint'. Even a one-pixel change creates a totally different ID.

timestamp.insight: Merkle Anchoring: We bundle hashes into a Merkle Tree and anchor the 'root' to Bitcoin. One block confirms thousands of documents.

verify.insight: Mathematical Audit: Verification doesn't need Satohash. Anyone with the proof file and a Bitcoin node can verify the timestamp.

protocol.hashingText: Your document is processed into a 64-character SHA-256 fingerprint locally. No one, including Satohash, ever sees your content.
protocol.merkleText: Multiple fingerprints are combined into a Merkle Tree. This allows for massive scaling and ensures absolute privacy in the proof.
protocol.anchorText: The Merkle Root is embedded into the Bitcoin blockchain. The transaction block height becomes your permanent, unforgeable timestamp.
